1.pericope_label: Moreover the Lord said unto me, Take thee a great roll, and write in it with a man pen concerning Maher-shalal-hash-baz
debates: Whether the writing surface is a roll or a tablet
Whether the birth was an actual event or a vision
How an idolatrous priest can be called a faithful witness
outliers: Calvin holds that the birth came to the prophet in a vision, since it is improbable the name was ever given to a real man, though he grants there would be no absurdity in a real son and will not argue hard against it

Calvin says the prophet looked not at the man but at the office, which made the testimony of an apostate priest free from every objection, while Henry allows that no exception lay against him as a witness
Ellicott takes the surface for a large tablet rather than a roll, noting the noun is the one used earlier for mirrors, and the writing for a common workman hand of the kind used on sign-boards
themes: A prophecy written large enough to be read at a distance
Four words a passer-by could carry home
A lifeless tablet replaced by a living one
A boy whose name announces the spoil every time it is spoken

4.pericope_label: Forasmuch as this people refuseth the waters of Shiloah that go softly, and rejoice in Rezin and Remaliah son
debates: Which child sets the time limit
Whether this people means Israel or Judah
What the two waters stand for
outliers: Calvin takes the child not as the prophet own son but as all children born about that time, against Gill, Ellicott and Wesley who read the boy just named

Ellicott suggests the unpopularity of Ahaz had made his own subjects welcome the invaders, so that the alliance was sought against them as much as against the confederates, and says the prophet takes neither side

Clarke sets two Roman poets beside the prophet, one on a foreign river discharging into the Tiber and one on a humbled Euphrates, and judges their uncontrasted figures unable to contend with his paired one
themes: A prophecy timed by a child first words
A gentle brook set against a flooding river
A king seeking foreign help against his own people
Envy of a neighbour stronger army

7.pericope_label: Now therefore, behold, the Lord bringeth up upon them the waters of the river, strong and many, even the king of Assyria, and all his glory
debates: Why the great river was envied
What the neck of the flood stands for
Whether the closing address names the child or the Christ
outliers: Calvin answers the wish with the threat, that a people envying a powerful king will be shown what it is to have one, since the more powerful kings are the more grievously they oppress and the less they restrain themselves
Calvin guards his own rule by adding that the prophet does not condemn human aid but the fear that drives men to distrust, so that help, if we have it, may lawfully be used
Ellicott takes the closing name of the earthly child and Calvin takes it of Christ, reading it as consolation that the desolation will not prevent the coming of the Redeemer
themes: A nation envying its neighbour emperor
A metaphor set inside a metaphor
Water at the neck and the capital in danger
A wasted land that still belongs to its owner

9.pericope_label: Associate yourselves, O ye people, and ye shall be broken in pieces; and give ear, all ye of far countries: gird yourselves, and ye shall be broken in pieces
debates: What the opening verb means
Whether the peoples are the confederates or all nations
On what ground the boast that God is with us may be made
outliers: Clarke follows the Septuagint in reading a call to know rather than to associate, noting the parallel with give ear in the next line and that Archbishop Secker approves the change, while Keil and Delitzsch reject the association sense the Targum adopts and read a summons to exasperate themselves
Calvin warns that wicked men also boast that God is with them and grow insolent on it, so that the boast is idle unless it rests on the word and proceeds from true faith
Calvin answers the question why peoples are addressed by noting that the invading army was made up of many nations, or that the prophet looks past this stroke to the incessant contests still to come
themes: A silent prayer turning into open defiance
A prophet on a watch-tower forgetting his own distress
Pains taken to roll a stone that will return on the roller
Attempts that are themselves the ruin of those who make them

11.pericope_label: For the Lord spake thus to me with a strong hand, and instructed me that I should not walk in the way of this people, saying, Say ye not, A confederacy, to all them to whom this people shall say, A confederacy
debates: What the strong hand describes
What the people are told not to say
What it means to sanctify the Lord
outliers: Clarke adopts a conjecture of Archbishop Secker, offered with great diffidence and almost withdrawn for want of authority, that the disputed word should be read as holy, since the two differ by transposing letters hardly distinguishable in many copies
Ellicott lists three readings of the disputed word and prefers the charge of conspiracy raised by the pro-Assyrian party against the prophet and his followers
Calvin thinks the commentators have missed the figure of the strong hand, which is a teacher seizing the hand of a pupil whose words have not taken effect, and holding it fast to compel obedience
themes: A servant of God held to his duty by force
Public opinion as a cloak for what is plainly wrong
Fear allowed but terror forbidden
A God conceived as a dead idol

14.pericope_label: And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem
debates: Who or what the sanctuary is
Whether the two houses divide the godly from the unbelieving
Whether the fall described is final
outliers: Calvin denies the reading that makes God partly a sanctuary and partly a stone according to which house is meant, holding that both kingdoms are named because the whole nation is meant
Clarke judges the words unto you necessary to the sense and lost from the text, preferring the Vulgate reading over emending sanctuary to snare or following the Chaldee judgment
Ellicott joins the two halves by making the stone the threshold of the sanctuary, so that the same stone is asylum to the seeing and a stumbling block to the blind
themes: A sanctuary that is also a citadel
A threshold stone that saves or trips according to the eye
An animal in a trap waiting for a helper
Bruised but not ground to powder

16.pericope_label: Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples. And I will wait upon the Lord, that hideth his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him
debates: Whose words the command is
What binding and sealing describe
Why the prophet waits rather than enquires
outliers: Gill denies that these are the words of the prophet, as Kimchi held, making them the words of the Lord to him, and Ellicott agrees that God is the speaker
Calvin makes the word a letter which many handle but only the addressee reads, and defends the rendering bind from the ancient custom of tying a thread round a letter before sealing it
Clarke reports from Bishop Chandler, by way of Archbishop Secker, that the Septuagint appear to have read a different word here, meaning that it be not understood
themes: A letter that stays shut to everyone but its addressee
A proclamation sealed under the broad seal
Faith shaken worst when enemies take the name of the Church
Grace hidden behind the wrath

18.pericope_label: Behold, I and the children whom the Lord hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from the Lord of hosts, which dwelleth in mount Zion
debates: Who is speaking of himself and his children
What the signs and wonders are
Whether the question about seeking God argues from the nations or from Israel
outliers: Gill takes the words as those of Christ and his spiritual offspring, Wesley as the prophet literally and Christ mystically, Calvin and Ellicott as the prophet alone; and Ellicott adds that the New Testament citation chiefly shows how little its writer cared for the original sense as the context fixed it
Calvin rejects the reading that refers signs and wonders to miracles, holding instead that the godly are looked on with abhorrence as monsters, and not only by strangers but by their own countrymen

Calvin refuses the common reading that argues from the nations consulting their false gods to how much more Israel should consult the true one, which is the reading Wesley gives, and applies the words to the adopted people themselves
themes: Children given for something beyond family enjoyment
A teacher who goes before rather than sends ahead
A chirping voice that thrilled the nerves
Asking the dead about the living

20.pericope_label: To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them
debates: Whether the appeal to the law is an oath
What the closing clause about light means
What the people curse in their hunger
outliers: Clarke denies that the disputed word means morning at all, holding that it serves elsewhere for dark or obscure, so that the clause should say there is no obscurity in the word; Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch keep the dawn, and Wesley takes the darkness to be in the minds of the hearers

Ellicott reports that the abruptness of the opening has led critics such as Cheyne to transpose the last two verses, and suspects the hunger is figurative, a famine not of bread but of hearing the word of the Lord

Clarke retails from Michaelis a passage in the Koran built on the same figure of light and storm, and the story of Labid, one of the seven Arabian poets whose verses hung at Mecca, who judged no man could have written it without inspiration
themes: A watchword given in time of battle
Soldiers on a night march fasting before the battle
An upward look made of defiance rather than hope
A man already in the dark driven further into it
